newsitem.title: FINLAND: CENTRAL BANK BILL IS EMU HURDLE FOR FINNISH GOVT.
newsitem.headline: CENTRAL BANK BILL IS EMU HURDLE FOR FINNISH GOVT.

text.p: Finnish government plans to be in Europe's single currency are facing a first democratic challenge, in debate on a bill to free the central bank from political influence which some see depriving Finland of control.
A first debate on the draft bill ended on Tuesday with the bill being sent to parliamentary committees for consideration. It is due back for voting late this spring.
The most controversial proposed change is to the tasks of the central bank's parliamentary supervisors, who now play a minor but key role in monetary and exchange rate policy.
The draft bill says all monetary and exchange rate policy decisions should be made independently by the Bank of Finland's board of management.
European economic and monetary union (EMU) requires EU countries to grant their central banks independence before the planned creation of a European Central Bank (ECB) in 1998.

Opposition MPs and some MPs from cabinet parties said the bill would remove political influence over monetary policy decisions, and some claimed its sole purpose was to make sure Finland qualifies for the third stage of EMU.
But second finance minister Arja Alho said the proposal was aimed primarily at bringing outdated central bank legislation in line with the requirements of deregulated financial markets.
Another target was to adapt Finnish legislation to the demands posed by the ongoing second phase of EMU, she said.
"The third stage of EMU is a completely different issue and should not get mixed up with this," Alho told parliament.
Opposition Centre Party MP Mauri Pekkarinen, a member of the Bank of Finland's board of parliamentary supervisors, called the bill "indisputably a step towards EMU."

"If this proposal is approved, national political steering (of monetary policy) will no longer exist," he said. "Without EMU there would have been no hurry to revise central bank legislation," he added.
Alho responded by saying that politicians could in future influence monetary policy through regular hearings with the central bank governor.
"The tasks of the supervisory board will not be taken away. The only thing that will change concerns the operative decision-making," she said.

Ilkka Kanerva, MP of the government Conservative Party and chairman of the central bank's parliamentary supervisors, said it was "a distinct problem that EMU would ... transfer monetary policy authority to the European Central Bank operating at a supra-national level beyond political responsibility."
"The critical question is ... whether parliament will have any possibilities to influence monetary policy," he told the house at the start of the debate last Friday.
Parliament's constitutional committee has been asked to rule whether the change in the tasks of the supervisory board shall be decided by simple majority or by a two-thirds majority.
The government has said a simple majority should suffice while EMU-critics call for a qualified majority ruling.

The five government parties have enough MPs for a two-thirds majority but do not control the five-sixths majority needed to declare a bill urgent -- a step usually needed to enact at once legislation decided by two-thirds majority.
But in this case, the international obligation to harmonise legislation with the Maastricht Treaty's ECB directives would override the need for a five-sixths majority, an official said.

The constitutional committee is expected to present by end-March its ruling to parliament's economic committee, which has been charged with the task of formulating the legislature's response to the proposal.
An official close to that second committee said its statement, which will form the base for decisive plenary session voting, will be ready "at the earliest late this spring."
